div.ab: Tape No. 2 R. Date: 3/13/74 Interviewer: Jeannette Lasansky (J) Interviewee: Hilda (H) and Earl Jefferies (E) , with Merrill Linn (M) in background Place: Carroll, PA their home

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Right down by Junior Christian's.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Let me just see something.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Everything was put up and dried and hung up there six weeks and smoked and cured for the summer use. And fresh meat like the tenderloin which you buy, like pork chops most farmers didn't make pork chops. They cut the pork off of what is even now considered pork chop instead of stripping the pig down the center of the back, they split it down each side of the back. And that would be boney meat and this lean piece which we consider pork chop now, was taken off and called tenderloin. Now farmers wives would take that and can it. Put it into the quart jar, process it for three hours, and pack it. Process it for three hours with a teaspoon of salt for each quart jar and that gave you your fresh lean meat. In the summertime when you wanted to change to the smokemeat. And that was a complete day's work. From early morning until daylight, until night. Of course they made scrapple. You've heard of scrapple. Take juice from the cannot meat and the liver and the kidneys, what else did they put in it? Heart. That all was boiled and the juice for that was what they made for scrapple. By putting white flour, buckwheat flour, corn meal in it. Sticking it into a wash type consistancy. Put it in a pan. Left chill and slice it down and fry it. That's for scrapple. And then the head meat itself was ground and put back into the kettle after it was all ground and a little of this former juice added to it. and that's what they have liverwurst. That they used to put in crocks, cover it with lard, and it would get hard and sealed up and you'd have that for months and months. In the winter time you used it for buckwheat, wheat cakes. For breakfast.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Pudding.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Pudding. That would be more pudding. That's liverwurst. Liverwurst or liver putting.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now is that different from what you would get in the stores? Liverwurst now and. . . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, the liverwurst that you buy now is usually a casing that you use as a sort of a spread. This pudding you can still buy it in the stores. Most stores you can buy liverwurst.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What is souse?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Souse. That was made from the pigs feet. From the knees down they chopped off the hoofs of it and those were strained and they were cooked so the meat was real tender. They'd take it off the bone and add a bit of salt and seasonings and the gel from that bone made it real nice and jelly like. You could slice it down like it had gelatin in it. You could never cook it though.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Was the souse and the putting and the scrapple used for different kinds of meals or different parts of the meal? What would be the main.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well, usually it would be the same as your main meat course. And lots of people didn't always make all of their pigs feet into souse. They used for boiled for sauerkraut, lots of times, too. They'd take pigs feet out for sauerkraut. Boil it in with sauerkraut. It was good that way.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now would the farmer when the pig was killed and begin to be sliced up, would the woman like select what kind of cuts she wanted? Could the. .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: usually she would. Sometimes she preferred to have pork chops. Well, then they cut the pig right down the center for the pork chops. usually they did it . . I know at our house they always did it the other way. They cut each side of the back. And then that boney meat which had nothing but nice lean on it that would make a good sauerkraut meat. Or turnips, or yellow turnips. They call them yellow turnips now. That makes an excellent meal. Cooking that fresh course with

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now your meat is then . . like your ham and your shoulder are they both ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: They are both pickled and smoked. And bacon, too. Usually sometimes often they had fresh bacon in our house. We'd fry it to a nice brown and then can that. After it was fried brown, fresh. And then you'd can that and you could use that in a lot of different ways. Heat it again. And lots of times you could put a piece of this fresh bacon over your baked filled mangoes, and things like that. That was butchering day. But that was a real hard, and then it was still a couple of days of hard work for the mother of the house because she prepared the fresh meets and things, and preserved them for later use.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would the cleaning of the intestines, would that be done that day?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. That was always done the same day immediately.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And that would be quite a job.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. Quite a job. Quitea messy job. And you learned how to do it. I mean I think I could still do it. You know there's just yards and yards to this intestine business. And you'd get it around your hand, you know and then you would have. . . This was my job as a kid, and it always was as long as I can remember. You take two strings and tie them just one here and one here. And then you'd cut between them here, see. That's the way you get the cut. It's a mess.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would you turn that inside out?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: you turn them out. You turn them and scope them both sides. Just strip those things up over your finger like that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about the stomach and other parts?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Now your getting to something that's really good. They take the lining out of the stomach, the front of the inside living. And that is to be scraped and soaked in salt water for quite awhile. And then it would be filled. The stomach would be filled either with sausage meat and stored away or smoked. Often times they smoked that. Also the bladder they'd use, believe it or not. Getting back to the stomach.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: O.K. I'm talking about the stomach.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You take the stomach and you have the two things you know, one here and one out. And you try to get this turned around without opening up all the way through, you know. Turn the thing inside out, the inner lining out and scope it real well. On both sides. And move all the fat deposits you can because along the edge of the stomach along the big end of it, there is always some fat. And after you have this all well cleaned and soaked in salt water, then you would make a filling out of it. Potatoes two 530 and partly boiled. Par boiled. And some fresh sausage, and some celery and if you like onions, or something like that you add a little onion, and bread crumbs. And you fill that and you cook it maybe for an hour or two. It would be in a pot. You take it out of the pot and you put it in an oven, and bake it for quite a little while. And then you would serve it, and it's very good. And very healthful. There's something about the content of the stomach walls that's good and healthy.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: How thick is that?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Some places 1/2" thick and other places, it's just 1/8 of an inch. You have to be very careful when your scraping it that you don't cut through and get it into holes because then you have difficulty holding your filling in. But those two main holes that you have you use to sew those shut with turkey pins. Sew it up with turkey pins.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Then you cook it for about an hour or. .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: An hour or two it depends. Put it into the oven and bake it. That sort of dries it up and browns it up a little bit.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So when I see in the supermarket, it says "Maws," M A W S; it's a stomach.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Try it sometime, I think you'd like it.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Were there ever parts of the body that was taboo to eat or?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Ah, we always ate the tongue. Either you cooked that or pickled. Or you put that in with your pudding meat. Or sausage meat, either one. But usually we pickled our tongue. They were small, but they were a choicy bit. We never used the ears. But they tell me now that they put those in sauce and things. And I'm inclined to agree with them. I found a few things in sauce that looked like ears. But they didn't used to do that, the home butchers.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: The tail?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: We never used the tail for anything. Yes, they did! That's interesting. . they used to make a 550 greaser with the tail. Cut about 2-1/2 inches of fat, you know the tail goes right up along the backbone, they cut the fat part out about 2 3/4 inches. And make a handle out of the tail, and they used to grease their griddles, their cast iron griddles.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Make a hot cake.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It really worked.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about the feet? Would they ever be pickled and just eaten alone?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Not that I know of. I think they may have done that but we made the souse out of it.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Was there any part that really wasn't used?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Nothing but the squeal.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: The squeal.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: The what?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: The squeal.
(H)The squeal was about the only thing they didn't use.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What's the squeal?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: eeeeeeee

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Oh, that part! The last thing! Was the head separated when you. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, they always cut the head off. They cut it off and take the jaws off, you know. And usually your pig's fat and he's pretty jump, and they take the excess fat off that before they cook it for pudding. But that's why pudding is awfully rich, it usually has regular fat; no matter how well they try to trim it off. There's pretty much fat to it. The liver. We always used the liver. And the kidneys of the pig, which aren’t too large. They were always cleaned and throwed in with the pudding. That was a real treat for the kids. That was a . . all the kids, if there weren’t too many youngsters, you divided your kidneys. You know they cut them in half and cleaned them. All the little webs and so on out of it. And the youngest always got a half a kidney. As soon as they were cooked, they run to the salt jar and put salt on it and eat this kidney. That was a real treat.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now the sweet breads. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Now that's something that I don't know much about. They've been. .. .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: The sweet breads are what? Is that the pancreas?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I believe it is. I believe it is that what we know as pancreas.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now you were mentioning that the meat we had today your . . . . is from your son.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's beef.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about that butchering was that ever done by people?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. Yes we used to kill beef at home. Raise the beef for our beef use. But he sends his to the locker plant. Now he doesn't even bother doing so.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Why do you think that the people that are still butchering pigs continue doing that?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: A lot of people like to de it. And the nicest part is home cured

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: ham. If they're done right, you just can't beat them for flavor. They're excellent. And if they're not done right, they can be pretty . . ah, not so good.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: The beef. Did a lot of people do their own butchering on that? How different was that at certain times of the year?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well, that depends on your beef age. I mean you wouldn't finish any- thing up in one day. You'd kill the beef and skin it, stick it and have it bled, the pigs were well bled before they were pulled up to the hog through. They always bled well.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What does that mean?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That means after you have them shot, stick them in the jugular vein. It makes them bleed out well.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: You do that when you are hunting for deer. Always cut the jugular vein.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Does it take very long to bleed out?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Not very long. They did the same thing with beef. They'd either . .
Often times they'd kill the beef by just taking a big heavy mallet and whopping them in the head. But usually they shoot them.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And then they'd let them bleed.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Let them bleed out well. And that either skin them laying down or else pin them up and skin them. But we didn't kill as many beef . . . while as I was growing as pigs. Because we knew more about pigs.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: With the pig your leaving the skin on. Your just taking the skin off.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Your just taking the bristles off.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What does the pine tar do? Do you know what . . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It somehow takes the bristles off someway. It has some good use in that. We used to have a man that made this. Earl was talking about that the other day. A man that rendered tar. I don't know how it did it, neither. Do you? I have no idea. I know that Dad and Mother used to buy it by the quart. In the quart can, Tobacco can or whatever he happened to have to put it in.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What would he use it for?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well there were other uses for tar. And I don't know what they were anymore, I really don't.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: I know there's a pine tar soap.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes. And that's very good. Pine tar soap. We used to use that for washing our hair. It was an excellent soap after you milked cows. If you got all smelly working with cows, you came in and used tar soap. You never could smell nothing of the barn on your hands. I always liked it for that purpose. That was before we had Dial. Or Irish Spring, or any of those kind.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: People would use it for their hair.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes. It was nice for your hair.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So a family, getting back to the butchering a family would kill from maybe 2 to 8 . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Two to eight pigs. And sometimes it would be two days of butchering. They'd only kill four one time and the other four the next time.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: That would be pretty much of a hard day's work.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. You had a big crowd if you had eight . . if you had eight pigs to butcher. You got them all cut up and the lard cut and everything it really was a job. We didn't often butcher more than six. That was usually about our limit.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about the lungs, are they . . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No. I'll tell you what they used to do with them. Everybody had chickens in those days. And they hang these lungs up in the chicken house. And the chicken would eat those lungs. They'd just pick at them and eat them. Or use them for fox bait. If you trap fox.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So, it sounds as if everything was used.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Everything was used. Everything except the squeal.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now the beef butchering, the hog butchering occurred a certain time of the year?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Always around November. Thanksgiving was a great day for having butchering. It was also a family get together. I mean they butchered on Thanksgiving Day and they had a great big meal, the table was grown with food. Of course by the time the men came in they were ready to eat.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Did the people smell a lot? I mean, were there any odors?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You mean after work?

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: From doing it. From doing it. Not from just hard work, but I mean from the butchering itself.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, not really. Unless you were real slippery about it. That would be the only reason you had a . . . .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: bad butcher.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: If I had a bad butcher and cut the wrong thing or something.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would that happen?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That happens sometime. It never usually happens to more than one person usually once. And after that they are pretty careful.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now the beef butchering would that be done at a certain time as well?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Usually in the fall of the year because of refrigeration. And then the meat would be cannot. Canned in quarts. And that really is a lovely thing to have on hand. Even now there's some people that butcher a beef

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: and they'll can so many quarts of it. You can get it at short order. I mean if somebody drops in on you unexpected, you have this ready cooked fresh meat to eat, and your in business. Another thing that they usually use is the entire stomach, the paunch, and make tripe out of it. Have you ever eaten tripe?

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Hope. I've heard it but I don't know . . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You've got a good thing coming your way if you want to try that sometime. Now

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now that's ah . . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's from the stomach of the beef.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Is that a particular part of the stomach or?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, the whole works. I know that mother worked for days in cleaning the stomach of beef to make tripe. And they can it and pickle it. Cook it till it's well done. And then cut it up in pieces and put it in a quart jar and then pickle it; like you would a pickled tongue or anything, I've always used a beef tongue.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: That's a much larger tongue than . . . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. In fact I've got some beef tongue out here, if you'd like to taste it. It's cooked and delicious.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: We used to have tongue a lot. I remember at I just wanted my father to cut it a certain way, otherwise you'd see some of the ruins.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's right. In here you’ll see this.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Yeah, and if he made the cuts as we were eating it, he'd cut it a certain way or you almost would have that . . quite a bit here, a piece of the tongue. But if he'd learn to cut it a different way only a few pieces actually had that. Now what did most people, has there been a change in diet, were people mainly beef enters or pork enters, or . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I think we were more pork eaters. I think more people have turned to beef in the last 30 years, than they did before. I think they . . in the country, I mean they ate more. More pork. Now city wise, I really don't know. Maybe they ate more beef there then they did pork. Maybe it's about 50 - 50.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now people are eating less of pork than. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I think so. I think people feel better on beef than they do on pork. I know.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Because of the fat.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: that we're getting older. That's right. Of course you can get too much beef, too.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: People would butcher enough to last for the rest of the year?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Last for the rest of the year.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would people buy cows or would they, would it be the kind of thing

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: that you would graze your own?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You'd graze your own. Usually you raised your own beef. Or some- times they'd kill a cow when she was no longer a good producer, they'd use that for beef. But as a rule they raised the beef or steer. Lots of times they'd make steers. Have a little special.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And would you say most people did this? I mean raising their own?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I think most farmers did, yes.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Even if they were farming for something else, they'd have enough?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: They'd either have enough or buy part of the beef or something like that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: We were talking earlier, you had mentioned the schnitz.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. Dried sweet apples. You've heard of that. That's a Dutch country... a real old Dutch dish. You boil a ham bone. After you get your ham sliced down, you just have a small amount of ham on the bone anymore, than you cook that and you add sweet apples, and then you make dumplings, and top it over with this can of apple juice. Put some nice brown sugar in the juice before you put the dumplings on and cook the dumplings from And you really have a feast if you like something like that. It's very good. And you use your apples without peeling them. You have to let the skins on the sweet apples. And that holds them together when they cook, so they don't crumble apart. That's an old Lancaster county dish, and an old Dutch dish.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do you dry both sweet and sour?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: We used to dry sour apples and make schnitz pie out of it. They called them schnitz pie. Or dried apple pie. That's something to do, too. That's done with the.. those you peel, the sour apples and then you cook them and mask them through a strainer, then you add sugar and species, and fill a double cut pie with them, and bike them in the oven like an apple pie. That's something else that is good, too.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: How do you go about drying?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Mother used to dry hers in the wood oven. Done mostly in the oven. And some people dry them in the sun. Because that time when we lived on the farm we had flies. We didn't like the idea of them being out where the flies could get on them. Because a dried apple will draw a fly very quickly.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would you put them on trays?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Put them on trays, they had like a window screen with wire nails in the bottom and my Dad used to fix those and you could slide them right in your oven. Let the one side dry and turn them over and keep on drying till they rattled.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Is this done on a low heat?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, a lot heat. You couldn't have them too hot, or they'd burn.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now what do you mean by a rattle?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well they feel dry and rattley like. When you knew they were dry

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: enough, you’d take them out and store them. Cool them and Store them,

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And when you go to prepare your food, how would you treat something that was dried?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You'd wash them good before you'd put them over to dry. Usually I soak mine. For the schnitz. I speak it for oh, maybe overrnight. And then wash them first and then soak them. And then cook them in that same water that they're soaked in. Add the sugar and dump that into the pan broth and put the dumplings on top and cook them for about 12 or 15 minutes. Then you serve your apples and your dumplings together and the ham.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about other vegetables or fruits, are they dried?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Dry beans a lot. I still like to dry beans. I Still like to have some and it goes with ham, too. It's a different taste than cannot beans. Yeah, we used to dry corn. And that's a lot of people are very fond of dried corn. I haven't dried any for a long time. A lot of people around here still do.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would you do it the same way that . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You do it the same way. You would do it in the oven.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Does it compare to your frozen or your canned . . .?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It tastes differently. You can buy it in the stores under Koch's dried corn. You’ll see that in your supermarkets anywhere. And that's made down around Lancaster county. And that's just about as good as you can bake. If we were hungry for dried corn, I'd just buy Koch's.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Is a dried vegetable or fruit, is it close to a fresh. . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, I wouldn't say so. I think the frozen can is much closer to the natural taste. Then what the dried is. The dried does something to it, but gives it different, it's good, but it's different.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: You dry the corn the same way you dry the apples?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's right. Even in a pie plate you can do it. Just put them on places and dry them like corn. Keep turning it from side to side. And about the early 20's they came out with a steamer, it was made out of sheet metal. And it was about 4 inches high, and had an opening at the top. Just like a box. And there was one opening at the end where you put water in and keep that filled with water and put your corn on the top of that. Now that did a nice job, too. That was sort of a steam drying deal. The only thing about that is I think your less likely to burn yourself. If your fire got too hot and you forgot about it, the first things you'd have a little scorched on the corn. And that does happen sometimes. Of course if you have happen to have a lot of kids around there's always somebody who would want to eat those scorched kernels.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would this be the kind of thing that, you know some of the other children would get involved in, or was it the kind of thing the mother. . .?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: The mother did most of those things and the older children. When I say about the scorched kernels, there's kids running around that would always want to eat the

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do you know anything about the days? Are there any streams with any natural clay deposits in this area?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, I don't.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Are there any potteries in this . . like in the Sugar Valley?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Loganton they made pottery, years and years ago. But that was long, long, before my time. Their pots are quite rare and quite expensive.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Is that a red kind of appearance?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, the crocks when they were finished they were just like an ordinary crock in color. They were gray.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Gray.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Gray.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do you know where there would be any information on the Loganton pottery? Anybody that you know would have read. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I think Ernie Geiswite might have something on... he's kind of our local historian. He knows about all those things.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: His name is?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Ernest Geiswite.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: He lives over here at east. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: And Merrill knows him.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: He's the last local history library on all of central Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You say you have?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: He does.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: He does. Ernie has a lot of information. He's about the only person I know that could give you some good information on it.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: O.K. Because when you say that color, that sounds more like a high fired, certain kind of days that would have that color. Most of them are low fired. They tend to be reddish.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Reddish. Well these that I have seen at Loganton were gray crocks. They had glaze finishings inside, so they were well made.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And when you were talking about the of putting in the crocks. Were most . . when you covered your crocks was that mostly with a wooden cover?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It was a wood cover.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Ever with like a cloth, ah . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well, when you made sauerkraut you put a cloth directly on your sauerkraut. And then you tied another one around your crock. And they put a lid on top of that. Because that was done to keep insects out. You know sauerkraut draws . . that was the main reason for that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And some of the others that you mentioned something that you put the lard . . over . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes. You put a half inch or so of lard over your liver pudding. Liverwurst. That would seal the crock and you could keep it in a cool place for a couple of months. And my mother as soon as she thought the weather was warmer in the spring you know; she'd get this crock out before anything happened to it, and she would can that liverwurst. Put it in pint jars. She’d put it in the pint jars. . .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: It was getting too warm?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, it would get too warm and it might be spoiled. She would take it in and melt it, you know on top of the stove. Like you would if you would want to serve it. And then she'd pack it in pint jars, and then process it in a hot water bottle. And then you'd have it any time of the year that you'd want.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Did sometimes the crocks have like a clay lid?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, I have one. One that Earl's father gave me. It has it's own clay lid. It's about three gallons. About this wide and about this wide. And I store carrots in that. I scrub them and dry them real good, and this year is the first year that my carrot's didn't keep. They simply deteriorated. I don't know what I did wrong, whether I had left them out too long to dry or, I just don't know. They didn't keep. And some years I've had them as late as the middle of March. I 'd go down and get a carrot just as nice as out of the ground. But not this year. And whether there was too much moisture in the cellar where I had it; I just don't know. But you can't keep carrots like that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do you know anything about the baskets? I've been interested in collecting Pennsylvania German baskets. Some of which are made of coils of rye. Coiled around, around, and around. And some of them are like hickory splints.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I have victory splint baskets, I have those here. Their made locals. But I don't know anybody that makes them at all around here. Nobody knowed how to do it, or didn’t want to doit, ordin't care to, or. . .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Were they made.. did generally most men know how to make them? Or were they special. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Just a few families knew how to make them. Heberlig and Esther Rumble made them, we had just mentioned at the table. He made them. have one of his baskets that he made when I was a little girl about 10 years old. And I still have it except that I don't have the He did very nice work.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So people if they wanted baskets would go. . these men say, were farmers and were doing something else on the side but they also could make. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's right. But usually these people that would make baskets, usually did not have large farms or didn't do much farming. They were lumbermen that worked in lumber mills or something like that. Mr. Rumble didn't have a big place, and Mr. Heberlig, neither one of them. They did nice basket work.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Did they both do primarily this splint. . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Splint work.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Did you ever remember of seeing them. . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, I never saw them doing it. I never say them working. It's kind of an art.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Yes. Their very nice and I'm just surprised that no one, that I haven't been able to find anyone. .. I found one person, a Mr Irvin, who remembers his father making very special sewing baskets for his two sisters, when they were going to be married. They were the rye coiled ones. It's kind of a fat coil like that that goes around and around, you know keeps on going around. .. .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes I think. Yeah, I think I have one here. They used to make bread baskets like that, too. They baked bread in them.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Really?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's right. They were called bread baskets. You've seen those that they made bread in already?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: I don't know that I have.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well, I hope I'm not misinforming, but that's what they told me that they baked bread in them. But they were made out of strands of lax or something. And then they had strip that wound them together.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I have one of them. Now, where did I put that now? I have it. I just took it off of the top of the. . Oh, no; I think I still. . . Good night! Somebody say something while I get this. Hurray!

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Why didn't that basket burn?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Well, they call it a bread basket. Maybe I was thinking of leaving it up here.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Yes. That's....

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Oh, yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: I think they served. This is the kind I'm talking about. The

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's kind of dirty.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: That this is the rye coiled and I guess this is hickory. Perhaps hickory again. And this kind of basket is supposed to be just Pennsylvania German. Where as the hickory split baskets, your shapes change from region to region. But their more universal material. But this is very much ah. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That needs washing. That came up from New Mexico.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: You get things that are very regional and then others that. . . We were talking about the distilling. Could we get on that?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You mean liquor distilling?

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I don't know much about that. I never really saw. . . .

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Well, I don't know too much about it, except hearsay. Well, more than that though. I found one. Hilda's Dad and I were sitting out here on the porch one day, and we were both forest fire wardens. I saw smoke coming up over here in the woods. South of here. So, I said to him, "that looks like a fire starting over there." He said, "never mind, don't pay any attention to it." So in about five minutes why no more smoke came up. So bird season came in and I wasn't satisfied. I had an inkling of what it was. So, I made it my business to hunt grouse over there. Here I came upon a beautiful still. Big vats. There were four or five big vats. They were at least three feet high. And about four feet across and approximately six feet in length. I think there was four or five vats that had the mash in and it was fermenting. And a big boiler there with copper tubing. And a nice spring run came down through the hollow there. That's where they'd run the water into the coils, making mash. So, the unusual thing about this is that you could walk within 50' of it and not notice that it was there. It was put in in the center of a big patch of rhodendron. And I fell unto it by dump luck. I knew it was over in there somewhere and I walked around this patch several times, and finally I saw where there was rhodendrons cut out here. So here they put a zigzag

path in the rhodendrons that you couldn't look right in through the still. It was zigzag. And I went over a couple of weeks later and everything had been moved out. There was a pile of coal there, and that explained the fire. They used kindling and so on to get the fire started, and that's where we saw the wood smoke, of course. And then when they put the coal on; why of course it no longer gave smoke. So that was that!

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: When was this?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That must have been in the 30's.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: That was in the early 30's. But nearly every hollow that had a good size run in, every one in these along this valley had a still in it some- time or other.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: When Earl used to come to see me out here in Buck's Gap why he could smell it. He could smell that mash.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: You could smell that mask. And everything along the run there. It was very unusual. The local people up there when I started to go with Hilda, thought that I was a rum runner! Well, nobody came in the valley who wasen' t. I was driving a Packard Fayette at that time. And it was a pretty fancy looking car and they had it made out that I was a rum runner. Well I left her place about midnight, or a little after midnight one night, and I got down as far as Steelton, Pa. And I was breezing through the streets there, I forget what time about 3 o'clock in the morning or something like that. And I was breezing down through the streets, and the first person I saw on the street was the milkman making a delivery. So I cut out toward Highspire, and the motorcycle pulled up along side of me, this cop turned on his siren and made me pull into the curb. I pulled over and stopped he said, "Your under arrest." I said, "What for?" He said, Speeding through town. I said, I was only doing about 30 or 40." He said, "Look on that speedometer." Here he did 60 or 65 to catch up to me. On his motorcycle. So he said, "Get out of that car. Left that front seat." Lift that back seat." I lifted that back seat. "What do you have in that compartment there in back of the front seat?" I said "That's nothing but a tool box. I keep the jack and the tools in there. He said, "Unlock it." So I unlocked it, and he looked in and saw nothing but tools. Then he got down on his hands and

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: knees with his flashlight and went up underneath this car. He thought I was hauling liquor. So it's unusual how you run on to information in later years. A couple of years later, I was working with a bricklayer from Steelton and I told him about this thing. "Oh," he said, "that guy." "Sure, he said, he was the biggest hijacker we had in town for years." He said "if you'd have had anything he'd have hijacked it." He was a cop.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That was in the 20's when liquor was in it's full swing.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: These had been regular legal distilleries before the prohibition? (B) No.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: He's the best darn story teller.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It didn't seem to hurt him too much. He was 82 years old.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: I didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It didn't seem to do him too much damage healthwise.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So before prohibition there were no distilleries here. And then . .

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Sure there were. There were places to lent them. They were illegal.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: They were legal then.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: No, they were illegal then. They are always illegal.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: They are always illegal.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: But it proliferated. Can you describe what it was like then?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Doing prohibition it became more prevalent.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And Prince Farington he came up...

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: From one of the southern states, I think one of The Carolinas. And taught these local fellows These men are both dead.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Why would he come up to this area, was there any particular reason?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: He was out of the way.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: He was in an isolated area to a point.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: At that time the roads into this valley were just this narrowest road down here.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It was in terrible shape.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: It was in terrible shape.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: This one wasen’t so hot.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: This one wasen't so good. Over to Jersey Shore.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: The forester roads weren't even made.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: They weren't even made, that's right. Rather an isolated section.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So, it was ideal to do something like that.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: The young people were in a depressed state too; because the lumbering was all gone, and they really didn't have much to go on except what they raised on their land.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Some of us were pretty poor.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So when you say that you could almost find a still in every hollow, I mean; what kind of numbers are you even talking about? Dozens?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: In this valley? There were dozens in this valley.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Sure there were. All these gaps between the mountains; they nearly have a stream, a mountain stream coming down through it. That made an ideal location for putting in a still. Maybe they would have one in here for a year or so, and the next thing they would move it out and put it in another gap somewhere.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would they move so they wouldn’t be caught?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Evidently.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Actually we don't know that much about it. He knows more about it than I do.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Boy was he being careful about not being caught!

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: But I'll tell you I was driving up and we were living up on the lodge and I was driving back and forth. And you know this stuff was going on. And me, the dumb thing, I never knew it. I really didn't.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: I didn't find out much about it till later.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, and the only thing you did; Ed came up one night to see if maybe you knew what funny smell was down there across this run.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: That was at Buck's Gap.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Buck's Gap. That's right. You did. But I was driving back and forth and I couldn't figure what was going on. They always did it after hours that I'd be home, I guess. Right in the middle of the day.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Well you said you could smell it?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: We smiled the mash. They dumped the mash right in the stream. And when it came down they claim that the trout get very big and fat on this mash that got discarded.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Now the time that this was discovered that one is this why it probably wasen't there the next time?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: No. I don't know. I don't think my presence there had one thing to do with it one way or the other.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: But by the same token you don't know, either. But because you remember how Uncle Hen was mixed up in this. My uncle. Madeline's husband. He was a widower and he was involved in taking care of a still up in this area. He watched a bunch of fellows come in and look the place over one time and he never showed up. He told us afterwards. So, you might have been seen going in there, too. You don't know.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: They might have kept people watching?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, they did in this particular case where Uncle Henry lived.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: I'll never forget. Fred said that Uncle Henry's up here watching this one. And he was shaving himself. He had a mirror nailed up to the tree there, and he had a straight favor, he was shaving himself. Fred sheaked up in back of him and said, "Be careful youdon't cut yourself.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: You didn't know my brother Fred?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: No, I never did.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: You said that Judge Johnson had bought your home.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Back in 1928 that was.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And I heard that he had delivered it right at the time this was all going on. When did he end the judgeship?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Along sometime in the forties. Wasen't it the forties?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: He resigned. It was before '45. He resigned to prevent the Senate from... What were they going to do with Nixon?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Impeach him.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Oh, impeach him. Johnson was going to be impeached. By the Senate.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: By the state senate?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: No.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Why?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: He was a federal judge.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What were the grounds?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: That's all in history.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: All right, I'll go look at the history book. From what date would I look u p on this?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Well I'll tell you the Scranton paper was supposed to have. . Look in the Scranton paper.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What in the thirties?

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Between'30 and 40.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Between '30 and '44.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: 14 years of papers. O.K.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: They were outspoken.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about burials? You were talking about the markers up in the ceme- teries?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, the ones up here. It had been a church there at one time. It had burned down apparently by lightning. Many years ago. And that has a lot of markers.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Are these fairly large?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Fla tstones are usually about that high, aren't they? Sand stones.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Were they ever carved or were they just placed . . ?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Some of them were. Somme of them didn't have anything on them at all.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: And I think that my great grandfather was one of those that was marked there.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: It doesn't have anything on that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do you know would they have carved an epitath? They never got that . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: They never got that far in carving. Most of those stones were a lot of the old cobblestones.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Were there any of sort of the old time burial traditions? Any thing in this area that you know of?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, not that I know of. I know when my grandma died, she was the first person I came in brush with death. My first was back in 1918. The hearse was drawn by horses at that time. But nothing unusual that I know of. They always had the body out in the home and the undertaker came there and picked it up at the church. Have the services at the church and . . . Everybody was practically laid out in there home, they didn't have a funeral home. That I remember very well. Now here totally I would say about 35 years. About 40 years maybe.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Prior to that they didn't have embombing did they?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, they embombed my grandma back in 1918. I think they did even with my grandparents, Zimmerman.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: They did that in the home.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: All the children and all they embombed when they died.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Did they ever put pennies... the old fashioned pennies on their lids?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, they did that. I often heard. I never saw it. They put it on their eyes from popping back open.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Is that your grandfather Hooker?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Now they could have done that to my grandma, but I didn't see her till she was rest. That's where your washroom is, that was where she was laid out. It was my first brush with death and I was scared to death. Mother said ,"now let s get over this right now." You come along back with me and I want you to put your hand on grandma's face. I did and I never had fear of death since. She said, "That will settle it." She said, "you won't be scared no more." And I haven't. I go over when somebody's dead and I touch them.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: There's some of the German superstitions.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's right. It took mother though, with her level head. Now that's what I'd do with my grandchildren. I'd do the same with my children. We had my father and my mother, my brother, and my brother-in-law were all buried from this living room here. When our kids were small, I'd take them up and have them touch. And my grandchildren don't have much chance. Because you know you don't get so much chance to do that in a funeral home, as you do in your own home. Our boys they were little when my father was laying dead, and my mother too. They came in here, you remember how they came in Earl? All the while they were here they were preparing them for the casket.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about the maple sugaring? In this area?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Oh, it's endless.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: We used to do that at home a lot. Daddy would carve little spots out of wood. He took a chisel and a chifel spout. And he took wood and he took a piece of wood about this big square.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: About an inch square.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: About this square. And he'd riddle off with his knife, and he'd fit it into the tree. They had rubber on and they had to fit it into that. They came in and put it down on the stove. We boiled it till it got to be nice sugar. And our kids did it while they were little. Our youngest son is in the insurance business, and how many gallon did they say they did this year?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Two gallon.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Two gallon. I mean they boiled down. . .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Down to two. . .

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: To get two gallon. .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: About how many?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Forty gallons to a gallon. Forty gallons of sap to a gallon of syrup.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's why it's so expensive. Now Tom is doing their's outside with a fire.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Is it a long process of doing it?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It takes quite a while.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: It takes a lot of heat.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would it take all day to. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: How would you go about identifying the tree? The Sugar Maple?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: The bark mostly. You can tell it by the bark. There's different types of sugar maple, red maple.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Sugar maple

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: And they have some real big sugar Naples in their lawn. Vermont has some though. (J Oh, I think so. Pennsylvania is supposed to be one of the biggest after Vermont and New York. Pennsylvania is one of the biggest. Do you know anybody that would be doing that around here, now?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Not on a commercial scale, no. I don't know any around here. Up around Potter county they had ah.. up around Cain that's. . . . Somerset county . . .

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: Somerset county has a tremendous maple sugar industry.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Maple sugaring, in Somerset county.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do you know anybody around here that we could. . you know that would be doing that on their own, that would?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, yes I do. Mrs. Boone down here west of Eastville. She's doing it.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would they be doing it now?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: They still were last week. I don't know how they do there. I think they have kind of a vat or something that they cook their's on. They did when John lived. I never got into it that big. We used to do ours on the woodstove.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Do people do anything special with the syrup in terms with any other recipes?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I don't know. I made some sponge candy this Christmas time. It was fairly successful. But I think they had a different kind of maple syrup then I was used to using. Because it foamed so terrifically when I boiled it. I tried to heat it the other week. Reheat it. Because it was out of a gallon container. And I thoughtif I reheat it and put it in small jars, it would keep better. And it foamed something terrible after it got hot. So I have never seen map doing it like that. It just foamed as if it had soda in it. So, I skimmed that all off and used the rest of the syrup.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about weaving and rugs, and spinning or dyeing?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Oh, no that was before my time. The spinning and the dyeing was. But braided rugs, they made braided rugs. I used to do it myself.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I would get scrap.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Is it the round oval. . . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes. The round oval. . .

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Like what I have my foot on. Is it that type? I mean it would look like that in terms of the form?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: You just saved scraps?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I saved scraps and maybe wool. Preferably wool. Because I think that does a nicer job. Where I think people are smart now if they go to these salvage stores and buy. . . these stores like Woolrich you can get pretty good material there. If you want to make a rug. You put all that work in it, and you take out worn material here; it's a lost cause. Because it doesn't hold up.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about the hook rugs?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I never booked any rugs. My sister used to.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Sometimes the booked rugs would have a traditional pattern to them.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I guess it's what you prefer.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: The quilting.. would that have been that you'd gather scraps?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That was made out of new clothes. It was new material. Quilts are interesting. I have some that my Mother made. I have some that my Grandmother made. And I don't seem to get time to do it. My daughter- in-law she made a guilt for her little boy's bed, and it's cute as can be. It's a little box about that big square. She started right in the center and went out in all directions with it. She just finished quilting it. But she didn't quilt around each seam. She quilted diagonal. That's a nice job. It took 6 months.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Did she do that in the frame?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: She did that in the frame. She bought a frame. My sister has given her frame to my other daughter. She hasn't had time to do any of it. We both know how and we teach her how to do it.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: I'm interested in a lot of the names of the quilts, and. .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: If you come again I'll have to find this information for you because Mother had a lot of quilt names. She has a bunch of them. A log cabin and a bear paw, and a monkey wrench and just a lot of different kinds.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Could she tell. . would she write down what the names were or would it be a kind of thing that she would just tell you or. .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: No, usually she had a clipping of it. A paper or magazineor something that she kept. I think that they are still all up there in a box.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Did she use patterns, I mean almost like a templet, a thick paper, or. . .

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes. Thick paper. Cardboard or heavy paper.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Sometimes I understand they used metal.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, I think that would be your best bet if you had a metal.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Like a tin.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: But it's a little hard to keep your material on that, too. Usually you should have something that should be pinned. I suppose that if you traced it before you cut it, that it would be all right.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Well sometimes I'll see a border where you'll have six lines going following each other, curving.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, they had a pattern for that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Would that have been a paper pattern or. .?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Paper or cardboard pattern. You'd mark it on and then quilt it. I think there was something like that the quilt that my sister made.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Sometimes they cross each other.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Two at a time. That's right. That was beautiful. There was a lot of work in that.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Was it sort of a pride in keeping your stitches close and your lines and stitches are not too far apart either.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That's right. You saw your lines and stitches together real fine. That's why I didn't like it. It was too tedious.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Friendship quilts. Did they sometimes have friendship quilt for people who would do different sections and put them together, or sign them?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes. Not long ago. That came in maybe 45 or 50 years ago.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So some of the history of the patterns would go back farther than others?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, I think so. And the ones that we had, my mother made for all us children what they called a Joseph quilt. No two patterns were alike, They had a triangular block, like that. What they called Joseph quilts. Each one of us got one. We have ours worn out. They made quincy quilts, too. You know where they used white wool..

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: And sometimes silks. Velvets.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: My sister made one out of silk where she took a square filled it with this thin lining in it, you know; and turned it over and joined the triangle. It was a beautiful thing. She put a ruff about that wide around it. That was a pretty thing. It should have worn well. It just happened that laying around that some of the silk would deteriorate. It was made out of , and the grapes all held up.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: Well I saw one quilt that I thought was made from a section that was made from used material. You don't think that was done, or could it have been done by somebody that was very poor.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It could be. And it could have been that old. It could have been a real old quilt. It had been used, maybe.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: It almost looked as if the things would have been used.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I have one up in my chest that has been used so long, and it's real old. And it looks like, like you say used material.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about blacksmiths or tinsmiths, were there. . ?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: There were blacksmiths here. There was a tinsmith here, too. Mulligan was a tinsmith.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Dave Price was a tinner.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: That was near Loganton. The blacksmith there was a blacksmith, Ernie Geiswite's father was a blacksmith. So, if you meet Ernie, he is the one that has historical things. He can tell you more about that than I can. But my Dad took his team over there seven miles to get them shod.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Ellis Laney . . . . There was Bill Barner.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: was the last one we had. He was down in Townersville. I don't know who does the work now that this riding club is in here. Whether somebody has taken up this. .

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: No, there's a fellow that comes up with a pick up from Lancaster county. He does the shoeing.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: But we don't have any locals around here anymore.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: We have an excellent blacksmith over here. He's filling in for Bill Barner.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yes, but does he do horseshoeing? He's a young man. He's taken up the . . he does wonderful work.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: So when did that sort of stop? They were doing just shoeing?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: I think Ernie's father went out of business in the 1930's. Didn't he Earl?

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: The later part of the depression.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: It must have been in the mid 40's when Ellis retired.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: Bill Barner passed away. I guess he was still blacksmithing when he died.

sp.speaker: Merrill:
sp.ab: It should be revived in this valley due to the large number of Amish families that are here.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: An Amishman would no doubt go to a blacksmith shop. Because we have about 18 families of Amish people that moved into this valley.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: In the last few years. And another thing I think that should be brought back is shoemaking. Shoe repair. That's really something to find a really good shoe repairman. But today people buy the cheapest shoes that they can get which they aren't the cheapest.

sp.speaker: Jeannette:
sp.ab: What about tanning?

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Not here. Williamsport had a tannery. North Bend had one.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: The factory site. At White Deer.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Yeah, there was a tannery there at one time.

sp.speaker: Earl:
sp.ab: A stocking factory; there was a tannery. Shirt factory.

sp.speaker: Hilda:
sp.ab: Up at the other end of White Deer. Right down by below Junior Christian's.
